title: The Hymn of the Ninth Floor
premise: Ada Okafor returns to the village of Hollowmere to bury their twin brother Emeka, only to find the parish records list Ada as the one who died twelve years ago. When the church bell—melted down in 1911 after a choir of nine children vanished mid-hymn—begins ringing again each night at 3:09, Ada realizes the village's oldest families have been feeding the bell a verse of names for generations, and Emeka's death was the latest payment. With three unlikely allies—a defrocked priest, a teenage archivist, and the last woman who refused to sing—Ada must learn the hymn's lost final verse, the one that releases rather than claims. In the climax, Ada sings the ninth-floor verse alone in the ruined belfry, trading their own name to free the nine children and end the inheritance; the epilogue shows Hollowmere silent at last, and Ada alive but unremembered by everyone except the found family who chose to remember them anyway.
about_author: Yara Halloran is the pen name of a former church archivist from the Welsh borders who spent a decade cataloguing parish bells before turning to horror. Their fiction explores what communities bury to survive, and what refuses to stay buried.

chapters.title: The Wrong Grave
chapters.summary: Ada Okafor arrives in Hollowmere for Emeka's funeral and finds their own name on the headstone being lowered into the earth. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: disorientation sharpening into dread—the homecoming that was supposed to be closure opens a wound instead.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: Alone in the inherited house on Ninth Street, Ada catalogs every noise they've rationalized since childhood: pipes, birds, settling beams. A journal entry from age ten surfaces, written in handwriting identical to Emeka's. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: the fragile architecture of denial beginning to crack.

The melted-down bell rings. Ada wakes to a sound with no source, counts nine tolls, and finds frost on the inside of the windows spelling a single word: NINTH. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: terror fused with a grim recognition that this has been waiting for them.

chapters.title: The Parish That Isn't
chapters.summary: Ada visits St. Brannoc's and discovers the church has no ninth pew, no ninth station of the cross, no page nine in any hymnal—all razored out decades ago. The vicar, Reverend Ilse Marsh, watches Ada too carefully. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: the sense of a curated absence, something deliberately erased.

chapters.title: Father Anselm's Confession
chapters.summary: In the village pub, a drunk ex-priest named Anselm tells Ada about the 1911 choir: nine children who climbed to the belfry to sing a ninth verse no adult had taught them, and never came down. The bell was melted 'to end the song.' POV: Ada. Emotional beat: horrified fascination—the first real map of the mystery.

chapters.title: The Archivist
chapters.summary: Sixteen-year-old Tovi Okonkwo-Bell, keeper of the village's unofficial digital archive, shows Ada photographs of the 1911 choir. One child's face is Ada's face. Another is Emeka's. POV: alternating Ada and Tovi. Emotional beat: an alliance forming out of shared obsession; the first warmth in the book.

chapters.title: What the Families Paid
chapters.summary: Ilse Marsh confronts Ada privately: the founding families have kept the bell fed for a century with 'tithes'—disappearances dressed as accidents. Emeka didn't die; he was given. POV: Ilse. Emotional beat: complicity and shame; the villain who believes she's a caretaker.

chapters.title: Ninth Floor
chapters.summary: Tovi decodes the archive: 'ninth floor' appears in every era's records—a workhouse ledger, a mine shaft map, the belfry ladder. The bell doesn't take people somewhere; it makes somewhere out of them. POV: Tovi. Emotional beat: intellectual dread crystallizing into resolve.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Refused
chapters.summary: Ada tracks Maren Voss, ninety-one, the last person offered the tithe who declined. Half her voice is gone—taken as interest—but she remembers the first eight verses and warns: never sing along, never harmonize, never answer when it calls your name. POV: Maren. Emotional beat: grief-tempered courage; a mentor earned through loss.

chapters.title: Emeka's Room
chapters.summary: Searching Emeka's locked room, Ada finds sheet music annotated over years—and a recording of Emeka humming the ninth verse, cut off mid-note. He'd been trying to end it alone. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: guilt transmuting into purpose; the twin bond reframed as unfinished collaboration.

chapters.title: First Toll After the Funeral
chapters.summary: The bell begins ringing nightly, one toll closer to nine each time. Villagers stop meeting Ada's eyes; shopkeepers refuse their money. The community is signaling that the debt remains unpaid. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: isolation—the cost of knowing, the village closing like a hand.

chapters.title: The Tithe List
chapters.summary: Tovi hacks the parish council's sealed minutes and recovers the full tithe ledger: names across four generations, ending with Emeka Okafor—and, dated next month, Ada Okafor. POV: Tovi. Emotional beat: cold fear becoming fury; the machinery of inheritance exposed.

chapters.title: Anselm's Last Mass
chapters.summary: Anselm attempts an unauthorized requiem to buy time and is found at dawn standing in the empty church, singing harmony with nothing, his voice already fraying. He gives Ada his old key to the belfry stairs before the silence takes him. POV: Anselm. Emotional beat: sacrifice and failure; the price of half-measures.

chapters.title: Harmonize
chapters.summary: Ada nearly answers the bell when it sings in Emeka's voice. Maren drags them back, losing her remaining hearing in the struggle. 'It always leads with love,' she writes. 'That's how it gets the second line.' POV: Ada. Emotional beat: heartbreak weaponized against them; the enemy's true nature revealed.

chapters.title: The Verse Beneath the Verse
chapters.summary: Cross-referencing Maren's eight verses with Emeka's annotations, Tovi realizes the ninth verse was never written down—it was split among the nine children in 1911, each carrying a fragment. The children aren't prisoners; they're the lock. POV: Tovi. Emotional beat: hope with teeth—the way out requires going in.

chapters.title: Nine Names
chapters.summary: The trio identifies all nine children from the 1911 photograph and learns their fragments survived as playground rhymes, lullabies, a gravestone epitaph. Assembling the verse means asking the village's descendants to surrender their inherited silence. POV: alternating. Emotional beat: found family solidifying; justice outside any law begins here.

chapters.title: The Council of Quiet
chapters.summary: Ilse convenes the founding families to force Ada's tithe early. Ada walks into the meeting and reads the ledger aloud, name by name, forcing the village to hear its own history. Some families defect. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: righteous confrontation; the moment invisibility ends by choice.

chapters.title: Retribution
chapters.summary: The loyal families retaliate: Tovi's archive is burned, Maren's cottage set alight. The bell rings nine times at noon—early, wrong, hungry. The rules are breaking down because the debt is close to collection. POV: Tovi. Emotional beat: desperation; everything they've built burning while the clock accelerates.

chapters.title: The Belfry Stairs
chapters.summary: Ada climbs toward the soundless belfry, passing landings that shouldn't exist—workhouse, minehead, schoolroom—each holding an echo of the taken. On the eighth landing, Emeka's voice asks them to turn back. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: love as temptation; the deepest test is grief itself.

chapters.title: The Ninth Floor
chapters.summary: In the belfry that is also nowhere, Ada finds the nine children still mid-hymn, held between notes for a century, Emeka newly arrived and already fading. To sing the assembled verse, Ada must give the bell a name of their own choosing—not a tithe, but a ransom. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: the climax—terror, tenderness, and absolute resolve converging.

chapters.title: Last Verse, Sung Alone
chapters.summary: Ada sings the ninth verse alone, offering their name freely—the one payment the bell cannot digest, because it was given, not taken. The hymn completes, the children step out of the note, the bell cracks down the middle and falls silent forever. Emeka's last look is gratitude. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: catharsis; the sacrifice that is also a liberation.

chapters.title: Unremembered
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Hollowmere has no record Ada Okafor ever lived there—except Tovi's rebuilt archive, Maren's testimony, and Ilse's public confession. The found family keeps the memory the magic erased. Ada stays, finally visible to the only people who matter. POV: Tovi. Emotional beat: quiet resolution—injustice ended not by law but by witness, love, and a name freely given.
